name: Pedro Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, and the first six weeks have mostly been lectures at nine, then the library until the light goes. I write everything by hand in A5 notebooks, because I remember it better that way. Tuesday evenings I go to the student union's tenants' group, and on Sundays I ring my parents, who run two pharmacies back home in Leicester.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose law, and what's it like living away from home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandfather was a bus driver and a union rep, and he used to say a contract is only as strong as the person who can read it. So I want to be the one who can read it. The flat is fine, I share with Tomas, who does engineering and lives on his laptop. My parents pay the rent and the fees, so I've no debt, and I know how lucky that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a lot of noise about a tool that drafts emails a bit faster. At the union meeting we'd probably argue that nothing changes for tenants either way. I wouldn't be shouting about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel a bit smug, because I never started using the tools and I'd have lost nothing. Law will still need people who can read a contract and stand up in a room. My worry would just be the ordinary one, getting a good training contract in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: lectures, handwritten notes, the library by eight. I'd apply for a summer placement at a law centre next year, because those are competitive. And I'd keep the Tuesday tenants' group going, since that's real experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world I signed up for, with the same worries as every law student. Some competition for placements, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never started using the tools. Would that change if some small time-saver did turn up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned never using AI tools. Would that change if a little time-saving did turn up? It might. If the university told us to use a research tool, I'd learn it, but I'd check every answer against the actual case, line by line. I don't trust a summary I can't trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents if they asked whether law was still a safe choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents if they asked whether law was still a safe choice? I'd tell my parents it's as safe as it ever was, and that the pharmacies are the bigger question mark with all the chains. My mum would say not to worry about her business, but she does.

say: I'd say it's **mostly hype**, a faster way to draft emails and nothing more.
At the tenants' group I'd argue it changes little for ordinary renters.
think: I feel a bit smug that I never started using AI tools and **lost nothing**.
My real worry is the usual one: winning a **training contract** in four years.
do: Keep **lectures, handwritten notes** and the library by eight as they are.
Apply for a **law centre placement** next summer and keep the Tuesday tenants' group going.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because this is the world he signed up for.
S0.quote: Law will still need people who can read a contract and stand up in a room.
fieldNote: Pedro's calm is genuine: **cushion and no debt** mean AI hype leaves him almost untouched.
He volunteers his own gap, no tool use, and says he would check any tool against real cases.

steps.text: Keep writing notes by hand and going to the library by eight
Apply for a summer placement at a law centre next year
Talk with my parents about how the pharmacies are doing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly the moment unions and regulators have to get involved, before firms quietly stop hiring juniors. I'd bring it to the tenants' group and the student union and ask what our university is doing for law graduates. I'd write to my MP if nobody else did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it unsettles me. The jobs that disappear first are the checking and drafting ones, and that's what trainee solicitors do. I'm top of my school results but that won't help if there are half as many training contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd stay in my notebooks but I'd learn what the tools can and can't do, so I could argue against them honestly. I'd push for the law society's student branch to ask firms how many places they'll offer. And I'd aim at law centres and human rights work, which are less likely to go to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for my family's money, but I'm uneasy about my own path. It's the feeling of walking up an escalator that's slowly changing direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if those junior jobs vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the juniors' jobs vanish? The firms, honestly, and the governments that let them cut quietly. Software doesn't decide to take a job, a partner at a firm decides to buy the software and not hire the trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that change for your first summer placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does that mean for your first summer placement? I'd start asking now. Last week I emailed a law centre in Leicester and the woman there said they never have enough hands, which made me feel better. Charities and advice work may still need people who sit across from someone and listen.

say: I'd say **unions and regulators** must step in before firms quietly stop hiring juniors.
I'd raise it at the tenants' group and the student union.
think: The jobs that vanish first are **checking and drafting**, which is what trainees do.
Top grades won't help if there are **half the** training contracts.
do: Learn what the tools do well, so I can **argue honestly** against them.
Push the law society student branch to ask firms about **training places**.
feel: **Uneasy**: his family's money is safe, but his own path feels shaky.
S1.quote: Software doesn't decide to take a job, a partner at a firm decides to buy the software and not hire the trainee.
fieldNote: Pedro's blame is clear: **employers and governments**, not software, decide who gets hired.
Outlook shows in his answers: unions, regulators and public bodies come before personal tactics.

steps.text: Learn what research tools can and can't do, to argue against them honestly
Ask the law society student branch how many places firms will offer
Write to my MP about junior legal jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the most serious thing that has ever happened to ordinary workers, and that we're not ready. I'd go to every union and tenants' meeting and demand a public plan. I'd probably say things online I'd regret, because I'd be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my degree might finish at the same moment the work does. I'd graduate in 2029, a year after AGI, and the thinking jobs I'm training for would already be gone. My parents' pharmacies might last until 2031, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating law as a plan and treat it as an education. I'd talk to my parents about whether they should sell one pharmacy while it has value, and I'd join anything organised: the union, a campaign, the party's youth wing. I'd also finally learn the tools, because being the one person in the room who doesn't know them would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can't pretend I have a plan, and two years is nothing. I'd still have money and a family, which is more than most, so I'd feel guilty about being this scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 2028 date change compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the 2028 date change compared with the slower pictures? It means there's no time for the university to catch up. Courses take years to change, and I'd be sitting in lectures designed for a world that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those two years? A guarantee that nobody is left without income while everyone sorts it out. I'd want it written into law, not promised in a speech by whoever is in power.

say: I'd say workers face their **biggest shock** ever and nobody is ready.
I'd demand a **public plan** at union and tenants' meetings.
think: I'd graduate in **2029**, a year after AGI, into jobs already gone.
The pharmacies might last until 2031, but **not for ever**.
do: Treat law as an **education**, not a plan, and join an organised campaign.
Ask my parents if they should **sell one pharmacy** while it has value.
feel: **Anxious**, with guilt about being scared when his family has money.
S2.quote: I'd graduate in 2029, a year after AGI, and the thinking jobs I'm training for would already be gone.
fieldNote: Pedro's anxiety comes from **timing**: the degree finishes after the jobs it trains for.
He admits he'd finally learn the tools, a reversal of his usual stance.

steps.text: Join the union and a campaign for a guaranteed income
Demand a public plan from my MP and party
Learn the AI tools I've avoided so far
Ask my parents whether to sell one pharmacy while it has value

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big change that we can see coming, so no one gets to claim surprise. I'd push for retraining funds and a say for workers before 2031, and I'd say it loudly at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is about my degree plus a very short career. I'd finish in 2029 and have two years of working life before AGI. That is enough to get on a ladder but not to climb it, and I can't see a good rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but shift towards the parts that stay human: advocacy, dealing with clients, tenant law. I'd spend each summer in advice work, and I'd save any money my parents give me. I'd also learn the tools properly by second year, because I wouldn't want to be the last one in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slower, like a weight in my chest rather than a siren. I'd have time to plan, and I'd hate that I might waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you? Five years is the difference between panic and a plan. In two years I'd demand things, in five I can build things. I mean a campaign and a record of work that shows I can think and speak in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the pharmacies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And what would you tell your parents about the pharmacies? Not to expand. Keep them lean, build up savings, and don't sign a long lease. I'd say it kindly, because my father (the owner) built both from nothing and doesn't like being told.

say: I'd say **nobody can claim surprise**, so we should demand retraining funds now.
I'd say it loudly at union meetings before 2031.
think: Five years is my degree plus **two years** of working life before AGI.
That gets me on a ladder but **not far up** it.
do: Focus on **advocacy**, client work and tenant law, parts that stay human.
Spend each summer in **advice work** and save what my parents give me.
feel: **Anxious**, but slower, like a weight rather than a siren.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between panic and a plan. In two years I'd demand things, in five I can build things.
fieldNote: Pedro treats time as a **resource**: five years lets him build, where two years would only let him demand.
Advice for his father is careful and kind: stay lean, save, avoid long leases.

steps.text: Spend each summer in advice work or a law centre
Save the extra money my parents give me
Campaign for retraining funds and a worker say before 2031
Learn the AI tools properly by the end of second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it on arguing about whether it's real. I'd tell people to start the political work now: tax rules, worker councils, retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel relatively fine. By 2036 I'd be 28 and have worked for years, and I could be in a role that's about people rather than paperwork. The pharmacies would have time to adapt too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, a master's maybe, and aim at law centre or policy work. I'd learn the tools gradually, with someone senior showing me. I'd keep saving, and I'd get involved in the campaigns that decide how AGI is governed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. It would be there all the time, like a deadline far off, but I'd have room to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still avoid AI tools with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you think you'd still avoid AI tools with ten years to go? Probably less than now. I'd move when it's proven and when the people I trust are using it, not before. Being slow isn't always a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd do differently with ten years to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the one thing you would do differently if you had ten years? I'd ask my grandfather's old union what rules they wished they'd had at the start. His generation saw factories change and learned the hard way, and I'd rather learn it from them.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** and we must start tax and worker rules now.
I'd tell classmates to get involved early.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with **years of experience**, maybe in people-facing work.
The pharmacies would also have **time to adapt**.
do: Finish the degree, maybe a **master's**, and aim at law centre or policy work.
Learn the tools **gradually** with someone senior showing me, and keep saving.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than anxious: a far-off deadline that still sits in the background.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it on arguing about whether it's real.
fieldNote: Pedro softens with time: he'd still be **slow to adopt** AI, but treats that as a choice, not a fault.
He wants advice from older union people who lived through earlier industrial change.

steps.text: Start political work on tax rules and worker councils now
Study for a master's in law, aiming at policy work
Keep saving what I can each term

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd be in my second year with a degree that might be worth far less by the time I finish. What would help is rules made early: a say for workers, and a public fund so the gains aren't all kept by a few firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm probably more stubborn about technology than I should be. I'd rather be slow and sure of my own thinking than quick and unable to say where my argument came from.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be slow and sure of my own thinking than quick and unable to say where my argument came from.
portrait: **Pedro** is an 18-year-old law student whose parents, who run two pharmacies, pay his fees and rent.
He writes **by hand**, refuses AI tools, and is inspired by his grandfather, a bus driver and union rep.
He blames **firms and governments** for moving too slowly, and wants unions, regulation and public funds in place early.
His mood rises with the warning time: **calm** if AI fizzles, anxious when his degree could lose its worth by graduation.
He is secure on money, but **stubbornness** about technology is the one risk he admits to.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, because his law degree might lose its worth before he graduates.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **early rules**, a worker say and a public fund so the gains are shared.
